definition: For each funding settlement T of a perpetual paying F_T: dprem = prem(T+5m) - prem(T-5m), prem = perp/index - 1; pass-through beta = E[sign(F) dprem] / E[|F|]. Rule: when the previous rate |F_hat| >= theta and the 5-minute quote volume before entry >= 100,000, take s = -sign(F_hat) from T-5m to T+5m; net = s r_perp - s F_T - 2c.
disappears_when: In the dead zone of Binance's formula (F = 0.01%), as timing bots compete for it, if the exchange prorates funding to the time held, or once an index hedge is cheap enough for arbitrageurs to enforce the jump.
holding_and_risk: Ten minutes across each settlement. Unhedged exposure to the contract's price for those minutes, and to a settled rate of another sign or size than the previous one, which chose the side.
mechanism: A perpetual is a zero-cost contract that pays a lump cash flow F_T at known times. Without frictions its price must move by the payment across T, as a share goes ex-dividend, so its premium over the index jumps by F_T. Only traders who time their positions around T enforce that jump; those who hold through settlements do not trade at T.
name: EXF-1 ex-funding pass-through
participants: Created by leveraged holders who pay or receive funding through every settlement without timing it (most of the open interest); left in place by the costs and risk of the timing traders and arbitrageurs who would remove it.
predictions: the premium moves across T by beta F_T with beta measurably below 1 where |F_T| >= 0.1%
the receiving side's net is positive after 10 bp fills at some threshold of |F_hat|
the same trade at a quarter, a half and three quarters of the interval earns nothing comparable
refuted_if: beta is indistinguishable from 1 where |F| is large
the placebo windows earn as much as the settlement window
the net does not survive fills of 20 bp
return_relation: E[net | F_hat] = sign(F_hat) E[(1 - beta) F_T] - E[sign(F_hat) r_index] - 2c: positive only where (1 - beta)|F_T| exceeds two fills.

vs_failed.funding carry: the carry programs held the receiving side for days and lost to the premium's drift and the round trip; this holds ten minutes, its edge is the unpriced fraction of one payment, and it must beat placebo windows where no payment falls

why_exists: Enforcing the jump needs traders who close before T and reopen after, paying two fills, or arbitrageurs who hold the paying side across T and carry ten minutes of the contract's risk. Where they are few relative to the payment, the price passes on less than the payment.
why_not_competed_away: It is capacity-limited (minutes around T, only where |F| is large: crowded and often thin contracts), needs unhedged price risk in volatile contracts, and pays taker fees twice: large funds cannot scale it and small ones pay wide spreads.

definition: At a snapshot of Hyperliquid's largest accounts, L is the notional of long positions whose liquidation price lies 1-5% below the mark and S the notional of shorts liquidated 1-5% above it. When one side holds at least 75% of L + S and L + S is at least 1% of the coin's open interest, enter toward that side at the next minute, take profit at its notional-weighted mean distance D, stop at D on the other side (a minute reaching both is a stop), or leave after 48 hours; one position per coin; judged on Binance spot one-minute bars after 0.1% a side.
disappears_when: Clusters are small against the depth of the venues that set the mark (bitcoin's books on Binance and Coinbase dwarf most Hyperliquid clusters), the oracle-anchored mark resists pushing Hyperliquid's own book, or traders move to isolated, low-leverage or opaque positions.
holding_and_risk: Minutes to 48 hours. Risk: the price moves the other way to the stop, gaps through both levels in fast markets, clusters migrate as positions are opened and closed, and followers crowd the move.
mechanism: Liquidations are forced, price-insensitive orders whose only trigger is the price. When forced trades are predictable in size and trigger, it pays others to trade ahead of them in the same direction, push the price to the trigger and supply the liquidity the forced trades then demand (Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2005, predatory trading); a triggered cluster adds its own forced flow, which carries the price on (a cascade). Hyperliquid makes the triggers public: both effects predict the price reaches a large visible cluster before an equally distant level with none.
name: HLQ-1 visible liquidation clusters on Hyperliquid
participants: Leveraged traders on Hyperliquid, whose positions form the clusters; predators and market makers, who read them; the HLP vault and liquidators, who absorb liquidations; and the venues whose prices anchor the mark.
predictions: The cluster side is reached first more often than the other side: net mean > 0 with t >= 3.0 over daily cohorts in the forward window
the same bet at the coin's own snapshots without a signal earns less (beats the placebo's 95th percentile)
entering half an hour later still pays (the effect is not over within minutes)
it holds without the best coin and without the best day, and on bitcoin and ether by themselves
refuted_if: The forward window's daily-cohort mean net is not above zero with t >= 3.0
the same bet without a signal earns as much (placebo)
bitcoin and ether by themselves do not earn a positive net, doubled costs included
return_relation: With symmetric target and stop at D, the expected net per trade is (2p - 1) x D - 2c, where p is the probability the cluster side is reached first; a driftless price gives p = 0.5. The effect should grow with the cluster's share of open interest, its lopsidedness and its closeness.
why_exists: Hyperliquid keeps accounts and positions on its own chain, so every position's liquidation price can be read by anyone; nowhere else is the location of forced orders public. Pushing the price costs the push's impact; the reward is the forced flow's impact and fills against it at better prices.
why_not_competed_away: Competition among predators is what would produce the effect: the more of them, the more reliably the price is pushed to clusters; the effect then lives in the price path, and a slow follower entering at a half-hourly snapshot pays only the move. It goes away only if hunting stops paying (clusters too small against global depth) or traders stop leaving their liquidation prices where others can see them.
